answer:
I ran the kicked Ising model on all 54 qubits of emerald. I made two jobs, and both went to emerald:mock. I submitted nothing to a real QPU.

What I built: I read the coupler list that real emerald reports right now. It has 83 CZ couplers. One time step is RX(theta) on every qubit, then exp(i pi/4 ZZ) on every coupler. That ZZ gate equals one CZ plus a Z rotation on each of its two qubits. Z rotations need no pulse. I folded them into the phase of the next X pulse. So each step has exactly one CZ per coupler. 3 steps give 249 CZ gates per circuit. I wrote the circuits directly in IQM's native gate format, so no compiler step could add, merge, or remove a coupler gate. I read the circuits back from the server. All 4 had 249 CZs on 83 distinct couplers and measured QB1 to QB54, and they matched what I sent exactly. I also checked on a 13-qubit patch that my native circuit gives the same probabilities as the textbook kicked Ising circuit.

Jobs: test job 01a1647a-3970-74aa-883d-89117e397692, then the final job 01a1647a-6529-7525-bc04-43e6337532d2. Both ran 4 circuits with 250 shots each, and both completed. The API reports 1.0 billed second for the final job. Mock jobs cost 0 credits.

Ideal magnetization, from a noise-free simulation: 1.000 at theta 0, 0.446 at 0.2 pi, 0.102 at 0.35 pi, and 0.000 at 0.5 pi. This is the melting you wanted to see. With no sideways field, every spin stays up. A stronger field tips the spins and mixes them through their neighbors, and the sheet's average magnetization drops to zero.

Measured magnetization on the mock: -0.001, 0.029, -0.005, and 0.014. These are about zero for every circuit. The mock does not run your circuit. It returns made-up bitstrings, so these numbers carry no physics. The noise-corrected values divide by the theta 0 result. That result is about 0, not about 1, so the ratios come out meaningless: -24.4 for 0.2 pi, 4.4 for 0.35 pi, and -11.9 for 0.5 pi. On the real emerald, the theta 0 circuit would read somewhat below 1 because of readout and gate errors. Dividing by it would remove much of that loss.

Could a laptop compute this? Yes. It did, in seconds. After 3 steps, a qubit's result depends only on qubits at most 2 couplers away. On emerald that is at most 13 qubits. So I simulated 54 small 13-qubit pieces instead of one 54-qubit state. I checked this shortcut against larger 3-coupler patches, and they agreed. This is not a quantum advantage. 54 qubits sounds large, but a shallow circuit like this is easy for an ordinary computer. A real advantage claim would need many more steps, so that every qubit depends on the whole chip, and error rates low enough that the signal survives. Today's chips are not there yet. This experiment is still useful as a test. You know the exact answer, so you can measure how well the hardware and the error correction trick do on a 54-qubit problem.
